model:vllm|title:warmctl fast cold start.content_excerpt: GPU checkpoint/restore for vLLM: snapshot a warmed-up engine (compiled kernels, CUDA graphs, weights, 1-8 GPUs) into an OCI image and restore it in seconds instead of a multi-minute cold start. Scale to zero, spot GPUs, Kubernetes optional. warmctl is GPU checkpoint/restore for vLLM. It snapshots a warmed-up engine and restores it in seconds on any host with the same GPUs and NVIDIA driver branch, so a new replica skips weight loading, torch.compile, kernel autotuning and CUDA graph capture. GLM-5.3-Flash on 8×H100: vLLM cold start 650 s, warmctl up 37 s, then stock serving speed. That makes scale to zero, fast autoscaling and spot GPU replacement practical for large models. The public catalog has 21 models on H100, H200, B200, B300, L40S and RTX PRO 6000. Any other model vLLM serves with sleep mode, build yourself ( tutorial ): warmctl up to serving, snapshot in page cache, against a vLLM cold start (weights on local disk, empty compile caches). ~ is the time to a ready engine while building the snapshot; where we measured both, a plain cold start was 1–24% shorter. On B200, GLM-5.3-Flash restores in 44 s (8×B200) and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in 73 s (4×B200). Every platform is in the catalog . GLM-5.3-Flash on 8×H100 by phase, from page cache and from a cold network file share (about 10 GB/s): Restored engines serve at stock vLLM speed or faster (GLM-5.3-Flash: 100–136% of stock throughput). build starts vLLM in a container, warms it over every shape in the profile and checkpoints the processes (CRIU), the GPUs (cuda-checkpoint) and the weights. push stores the snapshot as an OCI artifact, one per platform. up checks the host, restores everything at the same GPU addresses, runs a canary against the original engine and opens an OpenAI-compatible API. Multi-GPU engines keep NCCL and symmetric memory through NVIDIA cuInterpose. Details: how a restore works , architecture , shared GPU memory , registries and caches . warmctl is in beta: releases are GitHub pre-releases, and every user-facing change is in the CHANGELOG . Each restore is checked before it serves: the host must match the snapshot before anything is downloaded, every file carries its SHA-256, every weights allocation is compared by a GPU fingerprint, and a canary prompt must get the original engine's answer (bitwise for large models). story|title:agentguard transaction guard.content_excerpt: Transaction guardrails for AI agents that hold crypto wallets - simulate, evaluate against policy + reputation, allow/block/escalate with a signed audit trail. EVM + Solana AgentGuard is a transaction guardrail layer for AI agents that hold crypto wallets. Before an agent signs or broadcasts anything, it submits the proposed transaction to AgentGuard, which simulates it against live chain state, evaluates the simulated effects against an operator-defined policy, and returns allow , block or escalate with a human-readable explanation, a 0–100 risk score and an immutable audit record. Agents never get to decide for themselves whether a transaction is safe. It works on EVM chains and Solana, decodes the usual drain vectors (unlimited approvals, setApprovalForAll , permits, swaps with zero minimum output, SetAuthority, interactions with never-seen contracts), and ships with a conservative default policy plus a TypeScript SDK that wraps any signer so that signTransaction / sendTransaction are checked transparently. On top of the rule engine, a contract reputation layer ( @agentguard/reputation , in this repo) aggregates allow/deny lists, on-chain heuristics (age, proxy, bytecode size) and optional external intel feeds, and an optional behavioral anomaly layer ( @agentguard/behavior , separately licensed, see What's open and what's not ) scores each transaction against the agent's own learned baseline. Both plug into the same pipeline and both fail closed: an outage or an unreadable profile escalates, never allows. Everything in this repository is open source under the Apache License 2.0 : the shared types, the policy engine and default policy, the EVM and Solana simulation adapters, the contract reputation layer, the HTTP API with its tamper-evident audit log, the SDK, the demo and all of the tests. The behavioral anomaly layer is not in this repository. It ships as a separately licensed package, @agentguard/behavior , that learns a per-agent baseline (counterparties, amounts, cadence, approvals) from allowed decisions and flags transactions that are out of character for that agent, for example a $95 transfer to a never-paid address from an agent whose history is 30 routine $5 payments, which no static rule catches. It plugs into the open core without any code change here: The @agentguard/behavior package lives at https://github.com/Radmo3/agentguard-behavior (private; contact the maintainers for licensing). story|title:an ai agent said the code wa.content_excerpt: Agent A writes a change. Agent B reviews it and says it looks great. Agent A then edits one more file “real quick” and ships. Nobody lied. The review was fine. It was a review of different code. I have been doing this for roughly thirty years, and I can report that “the thing we checked is not the thing we shipped” is the oldest bug in the business. We have simply found a way to do it faster and with more confidence. I wrote Uncle ( github.com/unclehq/uncle ) because I got tired of it. At Yahoo I built Yahoo Mail's anti-spam system. Billions of messages a month, six patents, and one durable lesson: a component does not get to declare its own output trustworthy because it produced it. Spammers taught me that. Apparently it also applies to the thing we now let write our code, review our code, and then tell us how it went. Today's workflow: the agent implements, tests, reviews itself, and reports “done, all green.” Did the tests run? Did they finish? Did the reviewer look at the final code? Who knows, ask the agent. (It will say yes. It is very confident. It is always very confident.) A second reviewing agent does not fix this. Adding reviewers to an unbound review is just adding more people to a meeting that has already ended. A Git tree has a hash. That is a concrete thing to staple evidence to. So record that the review passed against a particular tree, that the tests passed against that same tree, that a human approved it, and then check, before publishing, that you are still holding that tree. Here is a real run from a demo project: The last green check is the one that matters here: the tree you are holding, 9edd…fedc , is the tree that was reviewed, so the evidence applies to this code. That is all it tells you. Two lines are red. The verification run failed (one command regressed against the baseline), and the adversarial-review gate was approved by the agent on nobody's behalf, because the run was unattended. Uncle prints both instead of rounding up. Also note the signature line: a signature is present, but with no trust root to check it against, it proves nothing about who signed. Verified , signed and a human looked at it are different claims, and the tool refuses to blur them. Revolutionary, I know. Change the tree and the evidence stops applying. The only twist is that the workflow has to enforce it, because “please remember to re-run the review” in a prompt is a wish, not a control. Same for the evidence itself.
